newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. Treasuries easier in Tokyo on UPS news.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries easier in Tokyo on UPS news.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were easier in Tokyo on Tuesday after United Parcel Service (UPS) said it had reached a tentative pact on a contract with International Brotherhood of Teamsters to end the Teamsters' 15-day strike.
Traders said sales by New York operators slightly depressed prices across the board, but the impact on Treasury prices was so far limited.
"T-bonds have come off a bit as the market was hoping for a long strike, which would depress GDP and non-farm payrolls for a while," a manager at a French brokerage house said.
While the impact of the UPS news was limited, it could have a bigger effect on the market later, traders said.

"I think many people were looking this as a symbol of what's happening in the labour market. The market fears that such an early agreement means the management might have completely surrendered to the demands of the union," he said.
"If that is true, then the market is worried that we might be seeing the beginning of the end of the long period of low wage inflation."
The benchmark 6-3/8 percent 30-year bond stood at 97-27/32, yielding 6.54 percent, compared with 98-3/32 in New York.

UPS said that under an agreement with Labor Secretary Alexis Herman, who has been pressing the two sides to make compromises at the negotiating table, no details of the tentative deal would be spelled out before Tuesday morning U.S. time.
Traders said they were eager to see the conditions of the agreement and that conditions could determine the near-term trend of the Treasury market.
The futures market also fell on the news, with the September T-bond futures crawling around a low of 113-27/32 by midday. It had been moving in a range of 113-27/32 to 114-7/32.
The market was expected to pay a close attention to price movements on Wall Street and to the dollar, traders said.

"T-bond prices have been firming in New York for the past several sessions, but underlying sentiment is still unclear," a senior U.S. brokerage trader said. "We should closely watch the trend in the stock market and the dollar."

The market was looking towards the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting later in the day, but most participants do not expect the Federal Reserve to tighten credit at this meeting, traders said.
